all_stories_flat.title: Story Of King Shahryar and His Brother
all_stories_flat.full_story: King Shahryar, ruler of Persia and India, discovers his wife's infidelity and executes her. Embittered, he marries a new virgin each night and executes her at dawn. His brother Shahzaman had similar fate. Vizier's daughter Shahrazad, learned in books and stories, volunteers to marry the king, with plan to tell stories and postpone execution. With her sister Dunyazad, she begins tales that last 1001 nights, each ending on cliffhanger.
all_stories_flat.source: Burton translation - Calcutta II / Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tale of the Trader and the Jinn
all_stories_flat.full_story: A merchant stops to eat dates and throws pits, accidentally killing a Jinni's son. Jinni appears demanding death. Merchant begs leave to settle affairs and returns. On his way, he meets three old Shaykhs each with an animal. They bargain with Jinni by telling wondrous tales, each tale buying one-third of merchant's blood. After three stories, Jinni forgives merchant.
all_stories_flat.source: Burton translation - Calcutta II / Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Fisherman and the Jinni
all_stories_flat.full_story: A poor fisherman casts net four times. Fourth time he pulls brass jar sealed with Solomon's seal. Opens it, huge Jinni emerges, threatens to kill fisherman because after centuries imprisoned he vowed to kill liberator. Fisherman tricks Jinni by doubting jar could hold him, Jinni re-enters to prove, fisherman seals jar again. Later Jinni bargains, leads fisherman to lake with colored fish. Fisherman sells fish to king, king discovers city turned to stone, etc. Contains sub-tales of Wazir and Sage Duban, King Sindibad and Falcon, Husband and Parrot, Prince and Ogress.
all_stories_flat.source: Burton translation - Calcutta II / Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Porter and the Three Ladies of Baghdad
all_stories_flat.full_story: A porter helps a lady shop, is invited to house of three sisters. They feast, but make him swear not to ask about what they do. Three Kalandars (wandering princes with shaved beards and lost eyes) knock. Ladies admit them with same oath. Then Caliph Harun al-Rashid in disguise with Jafar and executioner Masrur knocks, also admitted. Ladies beat dogs and weep, beat lutes. Porter and guests ask meaning. Ladies explain their histories: first lady was beaten by demon, second lady's tale, portress tale. Kalandars tell their tales. Caliph reveals himself and marries sisters.
all_stories_flat.source: Burton translation - Calcutta II / Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Hunchback's Tale
all_stories_flat.full_story: A tailor's hunchback chokes on fishbone and appears dead. Tailor and wife carry body to doctor's house, doctor trips over body, thinks he killed, drops body in steward's house, steward thinks thief etc. Body passes to many hands: Christian broker, etc. Each thinks he killed hunchback. Finally brought before king, each confesses. Barber called to examine, finds fishbone, removes, hunchback revives. King orders tale recorded. Contains Nazarene Broker's Story, Reeve's Tale, Jewish Doctor, Tailor, Barber's six brothers.
all_stories_flat.source: Burton translation - Calcutta II / Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali Raman and the Theft of Wells
all_stories_flat.full_story: One summer Vijayanagara faced water shortage. Tenali noticed wells drying not from drought but because palace guards stole water at night for merchants. Tenali placed chilies in one well, guards caught drinking that water were identified by red eyes, king punished them.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Two Thieves and the Royal Treasure
all_stories_flat.full_story: Two thieves boasted they could steal king's treasure. Tenali let them steal fake treasure chest filled with bees, thieves beaten by bees and caught.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Three Dolls
all_stories_flat.full_story: King Krishnadevaraya received three identical dolls from a foreign king who asked which is most valuable. Courtiers failed. Tenali inserted wire through dolls: first wire came out mouth (talks too much), second came out ear (hears but doesn't retain), third came out heart (retains wisdom). Third doll most valuable.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Horse Trader
all_stories_flat.full_story: A trader sold a weak horse claiming it was fast as wind. King bought. Tenali told trader to ride horse and chase wind, trader fell, exposed fraud.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Cat and the Milk
all_stories_flat.full_story: King's mother worried about mice, asked to guard milk. Tenali brought a cat, but cat drank all milk. Tenali said cat is like greedy officials who guard wealth but steal.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Dream of Palace
all_stories_flat.full_story: A courtier claimed he dreamed king gave him 1000 gold. Tenali said he dreamed courtier gave him 1000 gold in return. King laughed and made courtier pay.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Brinjal Curry
all_stories_flat.full_story: Tenali loved brinjal curry, his wife made excellent. King loved it too and forbade anyone else growing brinjals, keeping all for palace. Tenali secretly grew brinjals on terrace, wife leaked aroma, king smelled and caught Tenali but forgave after witty excuse.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Golden Mango
all_stories_flat.full_story: A miserly courtier never shared mangoes from his garden. King wanted one. Tenali told miser king would cut mango tree if he didn't share, miser brought mangoes. Tenali distributed to all, saying sharing increases sweetness.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Great Pundit
all_stories_flat.full_story: A haughty pundit from Kashi challenged Vijayanagara scholars, claimed title Tilakashta Mahisha Bandhana. Tenali broke the phrase: Tila = sesame, Kashta = firewood, Mahisha = buffalo, Bandhana = rope. He showed firewood tied with buffalo rope - sesame? Actually Tila-kashta... No book exists, just firewood tied with buffalo rope. Pundit was actually carrying firewood tied with rope on head, exposed as fool, fled.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Thieves and the Well
all_stories_flat.full_story: Thieves hid gold in well. Tenali told owner to worship well, thieves thought owner knew and moved gold, were caught red-handed.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Weight of Cotton
all_stories_flat.full_story: A merchant cheated with false weights. Tenali asked him to weigh cotton vs iron same weight - merchant's trick exposed because cotton looked more but weight same.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Horse of Two Colors
all_stories_flat.full_story: King's horse had two colors, artist couldn't paint. Tenali made horse roll in mud, made it one color, artist painted, then washed horse - trick.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the List of Fools
all_stories_flat.full_story: King asked Tenali to make list of fools in kingdom. Tenali wrote king's name first because king believed horse could lay eggs after trader fooled. King laughed, asked Tenali to add his own name if horse didn't lay egg.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Justice of the Parrot
all_stories_flat.full_story: A merchant left parrot to watch shop. Thief came, parrot screamed, Tenali caught thief. King made parrot court bird.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Arabian Horse
all_stories_flat.full_story: Arab trader brought fine horse for 5000 gold. Courtiers jealous said horse lame. Tenali proved horse fine by riding blindfolded - horse avoided obstacles by instinct.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Crows and the Scarecrow
all_stories_flat.full_story: Farmer complained crows ate crops. Tenali placed scarecrow that looked like king, crows feared king, left crops. Farmer rewarded.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Goddess Kali
all_stories_flat.full_story: Young Tenali went to Kali temple, goddess appeared with bowl of curd and bowl of knowledge, asked choose. Tenali tasted curd then said why not both, goddess laughed and granted wit. Later he became poet in King Krishnadevaraya court.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Painting of the King
all_stories_flat.full_story: King asked painters to paint him. One painted king taller, one shorter. Tenali painted king with eyes closed hunting - king liked because it hid one blind eye without insult.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Challenge of the Silent Pot
all_stories_flat.full_story: A merchant claimed pot could talk. Tenali proved ventriloquist hidden inside, exposed fraud.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Tax Collector
all_stories_flat.full_story: Tax collector harassed poor. Tenali made him carry donkey on shoulders saying king wants to weigh tax, collector embarrassed, reduced taxes.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Greedy Priest
all_stories_flat.full_story: Temple priest took all offerings. Tenali gave him statue that leaked offerings back to poor through hole, priest caught.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Magic Mango Tree
all_stories_flat.full_story: Tenali planted mango seed and said mantra 'I am fool' - tree grew quickly? Actually story where Tenali tricks guards that mango tree grows if you confess foolish act.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Tale of the Missing Gold
all_stories_flat.full_story: Gold coins missing from treasury, Tenali gave each suspect a stick of same length, said thief's stick will grow overnight by magic. Thief cut his stick short fearing growth, next day his stick shorter, caught.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Cure for the King's Cold
all_stories_flat.full_story: King had cold, doctors failed. Tenali made king laugh so much with joke that cold cleared with sneezing.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Persian Scholar
all_stories_flat.full_story: Persian scholar spoke only Persian, no one understood. Tenali learned few Persian words overnight, replied cleverly, scholar thought he was master, left gifts.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Donkey and the Washerman
all_stories_flat.full_story: Washerman's donkey lost, Tenali found and painted stripes like tiger, washerman feared, Tenali revealed trick to teach not to neglect donkey.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Dream Merchant
all_stories_flat.full_story: A man sold dreams. Tenali bought dream of being king for 1 gold, next day claimed half kingdom because in dream he was king.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Price of Buttermilk
all_stories_flat.full_story: Old woman sold buttermilk for 1 coin, courtier demanded free. Tenali made courtier churn buttermilk himself all day, understood labor.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Elephant and the Mouse
all_stories_flat.full_story: King's elephant scared, Tenali brought mouse, elephant fled, proving even big fears small.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Two Brothers and the Field
all_stories_flat.full_story: Two brothers fought over field division. Tenali said field belongs to one who can make it laugh (grow crops), judged by yield.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Envious Courtiers
all_stories_flat.full_story: Courtiers jealous of Tenali, placed thorns in his chair. Tenali sat, shouted 'Ah, flowers!' King thought courtiers honored him with flowers, rewarded Tenali, punished courtiers.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.full_story: Parrot taught to say 'Who is there?' Thief thought human inside house, fled.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Golden Bath
all_stories_flat.full_story: King built golden bath, Tenali bathed donkey in it saying donkey also needs gold bath to be pure like king.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.full_story: King asked how many crows in Vijayanagara. Tenali said 99,543. King asked how to verify. Tenali said if more, crows' relatives visiting, if less, crows gone to visit relatives - witty evasion.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The King and the Dull Minister
all_stories_flat.full_story: Minister always said 'Yes'. Tenali made him say 'No' by tricking with riddle.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Sword of the King
all_stories_flat.full_story: King's sword stolen, Tenali found thief by marking swords with turmeric - thief's hands stained?
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Tale of the Stolen Necklace
all_stories_flat.full_story: Queen's necklace stolen, Tenali spread flour on floor, footprints led to monkey who took shiny object to tree.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Ghost in the Palace
all_stories_flat.full_story: Courtiers claimed ghost in palace to scare king. Tenali found it was cat with luminous paint.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.full_story: Farmer's seeds stolen, Tenali made all farmers plant same seed, thief's field grew different because he stole different variety.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Language of Animals
all_stories_flat.full_story: Brahmin claimed he knew animal language. Tenali brought dog and cat, brahmin couldn't translate, exposed.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Tale of the Three Suitors
all_stories_flat.full_story: Princess had three suitors, Tenali asked each to describe princess without seeing, only one who loved her heart described truly, chosen.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Pot of Ghee
all_stories_flat.full_story: Similar to Mother Shandilee - Tenali's wife daydreamed about selling ghee and becoming rich, broke pot, Tenali taught lesson.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.full_story: King's barber cut beard too short, king angry. Tenali said short beard makes king look younger, king forgave.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.full_story: A rich man donated blindfolded. Tenali made him donate to poor directly, teaching charity needs eyes.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Tale of the Lazy Servant
all_stories_flat.full_story: Servant lazy, Tenali told master to pay him for sleeping, servant worked to avoid payment for sleep.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Woodcutter's Axe
all_stories_flat.full_story: Woodcutter lost axe, Tenali found golden axe and silver axe, woodcutter honest said his is iron, Tenali rewarded all three.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Tale of the Two Doors
all_stories_flat.full_story: King's palace had two doors, one for truth, one for lie, Tenali found which by asking guard.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the King's Portrait with One Eye
all_stories_flat.full_story: King Krishnadevaraya lost one eye in battle, painters afraid to paint. Tenali painted king shooting deer with one eye closed aiming arrow - respectful.
all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Challenge of Making a Rope from Ashes

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Flood

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Mango Thief

all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power

all_stories_flat.title: The Tale of the Old Woman and the King

all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Cursed Village

all_stories_flat.moral: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
all_stories_flat.source: Folklore - Vijayanagara Empire 16th century, public domain

all_stories_flat.title: Tenali and the Talking Mynah
all_stories_flat.full_story: Mynah repeated courtiers' secret insults about king, king punished courtiers.

all_stories_flat.title: The Fox and the Grapes
all_stories_flat.full_story: A Fox one day spied a beautiful bunch of ripe grapes hanging from a vine trained along the branches of a tree. The grapes seemed ready to burst with juice, and the Fox's mouth watered as he gazed longingly at them. The bunch hung from a high branch, and the Fox had to jump for it. The first time he jumped he failed to reach it. So he walked a short distance and took a running leap at it, only to fall short once more. Again and again he tried, but in vain. Now he sat down and looked at the grapes in disgust. 'What a fool I am,' he said. 'Here I am wearing myself out to get a bunch of sour grapes that are not worth gaping for.' And off he went. Moral: It is easy to despise what you cannot get.
all_stories_flat.moral: It is easy to despise what you cannot get.
all_stories_flat.source: Aesop - Townsend translation 1867 Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Tortoise and the Hare
all_stories_flat.full_story: A Hare was making fun of the Tortoise one day for being so slow. 'Do you ever get anywhere?' he asked with a mocking laugh. 'Yes,' replied the Tortoise, 'and I get there sooner than you think. I'll run you a race and prove it.' The Hare was much amused at the idea of running a race with the Tortoise, but for the fun of the thing he agreed. So the Fox, who had consented to act as judge, marked the distance and started the runners off. The Hare was soon far out of sight, and to make the Tortoise feel very deeply how ridiculous it was for him to try a race with a Hare, he lay down beside the course to take a nap until the Tortoise should catch up. The Tortoise meanwhile kept going slowly but steadily, and, after a time, passed the place where the Hare was sleeping. But the Hare slept on very peacefully; and when at last he did wake up, the Tortoise was near the goal. The Hare now ran his swiftest, but he could not overtake the Tortoise in time. Moral: Slow and steady wins the race.
all_stories_flat.moral: Slow and steady wins the race.
all_stories_flat.source: Aesop - Townsend translation 1867 Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
all_stories_flat.full_story: In a field one summer's day a Grasshopper was hopping about, chirping and singing to its heart's content. An Ant passed by, bearing along with great toil an ear of corn he was taking to the nest. 'Why not come and chat with me,' said the Grasshopper, 'instead of toiling and moiling in that way?' 'I am helping to lay up food for the winter,' said the Ant, 'and recommend you to do the same.' 'Why bother about winter?' said the Grasshopper; 'we have got plenty of food at present.' But the Ant went on its way and continued its toil. When the winter came the Grasshopper had no food and found itself dying of hunger, while it saw the ants distributing every day corn and grain from the stores they had collected in the summer. Then the Grasshopper knew: It is best to prepare for days of need. Moral: Work today for tomorrow.
all_stories_flat.moral: Work today for tomorrow.
all_stories_flat.source: Aesop - Townsend translation 1867 Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Lion and the Mouse
all_stories_flat.full_story: Once when a Lion was asleep a little Mouse began running up and down upon him; this soon wakened the Lion, who placed his huge paw upon him, and opened his big jaws to swallow him. 'Pardon, O King,' cried the little Mouse: 'forgive me this time, I shall never forget it: who knows but what I may be able to do you a turn some of these days?' The Lion was so tickled at the idea of the Mouse being able to help him, that he lifted up his paw and let him go. Some time after the Lion was caught in a trap, and the hunters who desired to carry him alive to the King, tied him to a tree while they went in search of a wagon to carry him on. Just then the little Mouse happened to pass by, and seeing the sad plight in which the Lion was, went up to him and soon gnawed away the ropes that bound the King of the Beasts. 'Was I not right?' said the little Mouse. Moral: Little friends may prove great friends.
all_stories_flat.moral: Little friends may prove great friends.
all_stories_flat.source: Aesop - Townsend translation 1867 Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
all_stories_flat.full_story: There once was a shepherd boy who was bored as he sat on the hillside watching the village sheep. To amuse himself he took a great breath and sang out, 'Wolf! Wolf! The Wolf is chasing the sheep!' The villagers came running up the hill to help the boy drive the wolf away. But when they arrived at the top of the hill, they found no wolf. The boy laughed at the sight of their angry faces. 'Don't cry wolf, shepherd boy,' said the villagers, 'when there's no wolf!' They went grumbling back down the hill. Later, the boy sang out again, 'Wolf! Wolf! The wolf is chasing the sheep!' To his naughty delight, he watched the villagers run up the hill to help him drive the wolf away. When the villagers saw no wolf they sternly said, 'Save your frightened song for when there is really something wrong! Don't cry wolf when there is no wolf!' But the boy just grinned and watched them go grumbling down the hill once more. Later, he saw a REAL wolf prowling about his flock. Alarmed, he leaped to his feet and sang out as loudly as he could, 'Wolf! Wolf!' But the villagers thought he was trying to fool them again, and so they didn't come. At sunset, the villagers wondered why the shepherd boy hadn't returned with their sheep. They went up the hill to find the boy. They found him weeping. 'There really was a wolf here! The flock has scattered! I cried out, Wolf! Why didn't you come?' An old man tried to comfort the boy as they went to bring back the sheep. 'We'll help you look for the lost sheep in the morning,' he said, putting his arm around the youth, 'Nobody believes a liar...even when he is telling the truth!' Moral: Liars are not believed even when they speak the truth.
all_stories_flat.moral: Liars are not believed even when they speak the truth.
all_stories_flat.source: Aesop - Townsend translation 1867 Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Crow and the Pitcher
all_stories_flat.full_story: A Crow, half-dead with thirst, came upon a Pitcher which had once been full of water; but when the Crow put its beak into the mouth of the Pitcher he found that only a very little water was left in it, and that he could not reach far enough down to get at it. He tried, and he tried, but at last had to give up in despair. Then a thought came to him, and he took a pebble and dropped it into the Pitcher. Then he took another pebble and dropped it into the Pitcher. Then he took another pebble and dropped that into the Pitcher. Then he took another pebble and dropped that into the Pitcher. At last, at last, he saw the water mount up near him, and after casting in a few more pebbles he was able to quench his thirst and save his life. Moral: Little by little does the trick.
all_stories_flat.moral: Little by little does the trick.
all_stories_flat.source: Aesop - Townsend translation 1867 Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Fox and the Crow
all_stories_flat.full_story: A Fox once saw a Crow fly off with a piece of cheese in its beak and settle on a branch of a tree. 'That's for me, as I am a Fox,' said Master Reynard, and he walked up to the foot of the tree. 'Good day, Mistress Crow,' he cried. 'How well you are looking today: how glossy your feathers; how bright your eye. I feel sure your voice must surpass that of other birds, just as your figure does; let me hear but one song from you that I may greet you as the Queen of Birds.' The Crow lifted up her head and began to caw her best, but the moment she opened her mouth the piece of cheese fell to the ground, only to be snapped up by Master Fox. 'That will do,' said he. 'That was all I wanted. In exchange for your cheese I will give you a piece of advice for the future: Do not trust flatterers.' Moral: Do not trust flatterers.
all_stories_flat.moral: Do not trust flatterers.
all_stories_flat.source: Aesop - Townsend translation 1867 Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs
all_stories_flat.full_story: There was once a Countryman who possessed the most wonderful Goose you can imagine, for every day when he visited the nest, the Goose had laid a beautiful, glittering, golden egg. The Countryman took the eggs to market and soon began to get rich. But it was not long before he grew impatient with the Goose because she gave him only a single golden egg a day. He was not getting rich fast enough. Then one day, after he had finished counting his money, the idea came to him that he could get all the golden eggs at once by killing the Goose and cutting it open. But when the deed was done, not a single golden egg did he find, and his precious Goose was dead. Moral: Those who have plenty want more and so lose all they have.
all_stories_flat.moral: Those who have plenty want more and so lose all they have.
all_stories_flat.source: Aesop - Townsend translation 1867 Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Wind and the Sun
all_stories_flat.full_story: The Wind and the Sun were disputing which was the stronger. Suddenly they saw a traveller coming down the road, and the Sun said: 'I see a way to decide our dispute. Whichever of us can cause that traveller to take off his cloak shall be regarded as the stronger. You begin.' So the Sun retired behind a cloud, and the Wind began to blow as hard as it could upon the traveller. But the harder he blew the more closely did the traveller wrap his cloak round him, till at last the Wind had to give up in despair. Then the Sun came out and shone in all his glory upon the traveller, who soon found it too hot to walk with his cloak on. Moral: Kindness effects more than severity.
all_stories_flat.moral: Kindness effects more than severity.
all_stories_flat.source: Aesop - Townsend translation 1867 Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: The Wolf in Sheep's Clothing
all_stories_flat.full_story: Once upon a time a Wolf resolved to disguise his appearance in order to secure food more easily. Encased in the skin of a sheep, he pastured with the flock deceiving the shepherd by his costume. In the evening he was shut up by the shepherd in the fold; the night and the fold were both dark, and the shepherd, on his return to the fold, instantly slaughtered the Wolf, mistaking him for a sheep. Moral: Harm seek, harm find.
all_stories_flat.moral: Harm seek, harm find.
all_stories_flat.source: Aesop - Townsend translation 1867 Public Domain

all_stories_flat.title: Yeh-Shen (Ye Xian) - China - Oldest Known Cinderella
all_stories_flat.source: Youyang Zazu by Duan Chengshi - Tang Dynasty
all_stories_flat.full_story: In ancient China, Chief Wu had two wives. One died leaving daughter Yeh-Shen, beautiful and clever at pottery. Her stepmother hated her and made her work in caves gathering firewood and water. Yeh-Shen had only one friend, a fish with golden eyes in a pond, which she fed daily. Stepmother discovered fish, killed it and ate it, hiding bones. An old man from heaven told Yeh-Shen to hide fish bones in her room; whatever she wished would be granted. New Year festival came, stepmother forced her to stay home. Yeh-Shen prayed to bones and was given a cloak of kingfisher feathers and tiny golden slippers. She went to festival, charmed all, but fled losing one slipper when step-siblings chased. A trader from To'han found slipper and presented to king. King searched for owner, trying slipper on all women. Finally Yeh-Shen tried it, it fit perfectly. She wore feather cloak again, king married her. Stepmother and stepsister were stoned to death? Actually they fled and were buried in flying stones in some versions.
all_stories_flat.ending: Marries king, stepfamily punished by flying stones
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.title: Rhodopis - Egypt/Greece - 1st Century BCE
all_stories_flat.source: Strabo, Herodotus variant
all_stories_flat.full_story: Rhodopis was a beautiful Greek courtesan living in Naukratis, Egypt. One day while bathing, an eagle (actually Horus?) snatched one of her red-rose gilded slippers and flew away, dropping it in lap of Pharaoh Psammetichus in Memphis who was holding court. Pharaoh, struck by small size and beauty of slipper, sent heralds throughout Egypt to find woman to whom slipper belonged. Found Rhodopis, married her, making her Queen of Egypt. Oldest Cinderella-like tale with slipper test.
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.title: Cenerentola - La Gatta Cenerentola - Italy - Basile
all_stories_flat.source: Giambattista Basile - Pentamerone - Lo Cunto de li Cunti
all_stories_flat.full_story: Zezolla is a princess whose governess kills her own mother? Actually Zezolla's father has new wife, her governess becomes stepmother with six daughters. Zezolla is demoted to kitchen, called Gatta Cenerentola (Cat Cinderella) because she tends fireplace. She plants a date tree given by fairy from Crete. Fairy lives in tree and grants wishes. King holds feast. Zezolla asks fairy for dress, goes three nights with different dresses, loses slipper - a patten (slipper) or cioppine. King's servant finds it. King declares woman who fits slipper will be queen. Stepsisters cut feet but doves point blood. Zezolla fits, becomes queen, stepmother punished.
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.title: Cendrillon ou La Petite Pantoufle de Verre - France - Perrault
all_stories_flat.source: Charles Perrault - Histoires ou Contes du Temps Passé
all_stories_flat.full_story: A gentleman's daughter after mother's death suffers under second wife with two proud daughters. She is made to sleep in attic among cinders, called Cinderella (Cendrillon). Father in her shadow. Prince holds ball for two days. Cinderella weeps, her fairy godmother appears, transforms pumpkin into carriage, mice into horses, rat into coachman, lizards into footmen, her rags into beautiful gown of cloth of gold and silver, gives glass slippers (pantoufle de verre - some say vair fur). Warns to leave before midnight when magic ends. Cinderella goes, charms prince, leaves at midnight first night, second night stays till clock strikes twelve, loses glass slipper fleeing. Prince proclaims he will marry woman who fits glass slipper. Stepsisters try to force foot, fail. Cinderella asks to try, fits, produces second slipper, fairy godmother makes her even more beautiful, marries prince, forgives stepsisters and marries them to lords.
all_stories_flat.ending: Forgives stepsisters, marries them to lords
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.title: Aschenputtel - Germany - Brothers Grimm
all_stories_flat.source: Brothers Grimm - Kinder- und Hausmärchen KHM 21
all_stories_flat.full_story: A rich man's wife dies, tells daughter to remain pious. Man remarries woman with two daughters beautiful but evil. They call stepdaughter Aschenputtel (Ashputtel) because she must sit in ashes. Father goes to fair, asks what to bring, stepdaughters ask fine clothes, Aschenputtel asks first branch that knocks his hat on way home. Father brings hazel branch, she plants on mother's grave, waters with tears, grows into great tree, white bird lives in it granting wishes. King holds three-day festival to find bride. Aschenputtel asks stepmother to go, denied, stepmother throws lentils into ashes task. White birds sort lentils. Aschenputtel goes to tree: 'Shiver and quiver little tree, silver and gold throw down over me.' Bird throws gold and silver dress and silk slippers. She goes to ball, prince dances only with her, she escapes. Three nights, dresses more beautiful each night, third night prince spreads pitch, loses gold slipper. Prince goes house to house, stepsisters cut toe and heel to fit, doves cry 'Rook di goo, blood in shoe!' Finally Aschenputtel fits, doves say she is true bride. At wedding, doves peck out stepsisters' eyes for wickedness.
all_stories_flat.ending: Stepsisters blinded by doves, harsh punishment
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.title: Katie Woodencloak (Kari Trestakk) - Norway
all_stories_flat.source: Asbjornsen and Moe - Norwegian Folktales
all_stories_flat.full_story: King has daughter Katie, queen dies, king remarries widow with daughter. New queen cruel, Katie flees dressed in wooden cloak (trestakk) with a bull that is her friend. Bull tells her to kill him and take items from his body: cloth, etc. Bull fights dragon? Actually bull fights other bulls for kingdom. Katie works in castle kitchen as Kari Woodencloak. Prince holds church viewing (three Sundays). Katie asks to go, denied, then uses bull's gifts: gets silver dress and horse, goes to church, prince falls in love, she throws golden apple? Actually she is seen. Third time prince puts tar to catch her, she loses one golden boot. Prince finds boot, seeks owner. Katie reveals wooden cloak off, shows she is princess, marries prince.
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.full_story: A king's daughter whose mother dies, stepmother hates her, has a sharp gray sheep (pet) that helps her. Stepmother kills sheep. Daughter weeps over sheep's grave, bird helps? She goes to church in fine dresses from sheep, loses shoe. Prince finds, marries.
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.title: Rashin-Coatie - Scotland
all_stories_flat.source: Campbell
all_stories_flat.full_story: Daughter of gentleman, mother dies, father remarries cruel wife with daughter. Rashin-Coatie is name because she wears coat of rushes. Has red calf that helps. Calf killed by stepmother. Rashin weeps, calf's bones give fine clothes. King holds ball, Rashin goes three nights, loses satin shoe, king finds, marries.
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.title: Ye Xian alternative - Vietnam / Tam and Cam
all_stories_flat.source: Vietnamese folklore - Tam Cam
all_stories_flat.full_story: Tam is kind, Cam is cruel stepsister, stepmother hates Tam. Tam has fish pet Bống, stepmother kills it. Buddha-like old woman gives Tam bones magic. Festival, Tam gets beautiful clothes and shoes from magic. Loses shoe, king finds, Tam fits, becomes queen. Stepmother plots, kills Tam making her reincarnate as oriole, fruit tree, loom shuttle, etc., each time Cam kills reincarnation, finally Tam reborn from areca fruit and reunites with king, punishes stepfamily by making them eat tainted food and die.
all_stories_flat.ending: Stepmother and Cam die after eating poisoned
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.title: Cinderella - Native American - The Rough-Face Girl - Algonquin
all_stories_flat.source: Algonquin - recorded by Charles G. Leland
all_stories_flat.full_story: In a village by lake, a girl is scarred by fire tending fire, called Rough-Face Girl, mocked by sisters. Invisible Being (mighty spirit) lives across lake, his sister guards him, only girl who can see him may marry him. Many girls try, fail to see him. Rough-Face Girl with help of birch tree and magic moccasins, with face washed clean by lake water, sees Invisible Being, wears beautiful clothes, marries him, scars healed.
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.title: The Baba Yaga and Vasilisa the Beautiful - Russia
all_stories_flat.source: Alexander Afanasyev - Narodnye Russkie Skazki
all_stories_flat.full_story: Vasilisa's mother dies, gives doll blessed. Father remarries cruel woman with two daughters who send Vasilisa to forest to get light from Baba Yaga's hut, hoping Yaga will eat her. Baba Yaga tests Vasilisa with impossible tasks: separate wheat, poppy etc. Doll helps. Vasilisa passes, Yaga gives skull lantern with burning eyes. Skull burns stepmother and stepsisters to death. Vasilisa goes to city, weaves fine cloth, Tsar sees cloth, seeks weaver, marries Vasilisa. No slipper but persecuted heroine motif.
all_stories_flat.ending: Stepmother and stepsisters incinerated, marries Tsar
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.title: Cap o' Rushes - England
all_stories_flat.source: English Fairy Tales - Jacobs
all_stories_flat.full_story: A man has three daughters, asks how much they love him. Third says as much as salt. Father angry, banishes her. She makes coat of rushes, goes to great house, works as servant Cap o' Rushes. Son of house sees her fine without rush coat when she goes to dance, falls in love. She reveals identity, father who now knows value of salt repents.
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.title: Catskin - England
all_stories_flat.source: English Fairy Tales
all_stories_flat.full_story: Similar to Cap o' Rushes, but also includes incestuous father who wants to marry daughter because she resembles dead mother, she asks for coat of catskins and flees, works as scullion, marries lord.
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.title: Nya-chan and the Golden Slipper - West Africa - Ghana
all_stories_flat.source: African folklore
all_stories_flat.full_story: Nya is orphan mistreated by stepmother, has no shoes. Goes to river, water spirit gives golden slippers that dance. At festival, chief's son sees her dancing, slipper falls in river, chief finds, fits Nya, marries.
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.source: Indian folklore - Sara Dosa? Punjab variant
all_stories_flat.full_story: A girl has anklet (payal) instead of slipper. Stepmother mistreats. Girl goes to well, fairy gives beautiful anklet. Prince hears anklet sound, follows, finds owner, marries.

all_stories_flat.title: Cinderella - Persian Variant - Moon-Brow Girl (Mahpishani)
all_stories_flat.source: Persian Tales
all_stories_flat.full_story: Girl with moon-like brow mistreated by stepmother, has cow helper, cow killed, bones become tree granting dresses, goes to festival, loses shoe made of almond? Prince finds, marries.

all_stories_flat.title: Little Saddleslut - Ireland
all_stories_flat.source: Irish - W.B. Yeats collection
all_stories_flat.full_story: Girl called Little Saddleslut because works in kitchen, has hen that lays? Helps? Goes to mass in fine cloak from hen, loses shoe, prince finds.
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

all_stories_flat.full_story: A poor girl tends turkeys, turkeys are magical, give her fine clothes of feathers to go to Dance of Sacred Bird, she loses? all_stories_flat.full_story: Stepdaughter called Benizara (red plate) and Kakezara (broken plate), works in kitchen. Has sparrow helper. Sparrow gives magic mallet and dress. Goes to festival, loses geta sandal, lord finds, marries.

all_stories_flat.source: Korean folklore - Kongji Patzzi jeon
all_stories_flat.full_story: Kongji's mother dies, cruel stepmother Patzzi and stepsister Patzzi? Actually stepmother and daughter. Kongji helped by cow, sparrows, toads. Cow plows field, sparrows sort rice, toads bring water. Festival, birds give dress, loses shoe? Actually governor finds shoe? Fairy helps, Kongji marries governor, stepmother punished: turned into pot? Death by sauce jar.
all_stories_flat.ending: Stepmother dies by falling into sauce jar or drowned
all_stories_flat.parent_collection: Cinderella World Variants - ATU 510A Persecuted Heroine

Nasruddin stepped in as judge. He took coins from his pocket, jingled them near owner's ear and said: 'The sound of money pays for the smell of soup.'

all_stories_flat.title: Thumbelina
all_stories_flat.full_story: Woman wants child, witch gives barley seed, grows flower, tiny girl inside Thumbelina. Sleeps in walnut shell. Toad steals to marry to son, fish help escape on lily pad. Cockchafer beetle takes her, finds ugly, leaves. Field mouse shelters winter, wants her marry mole blind who hates sun. Swallow she saved tells her to flee. Takes her to land of flower prince, Thumbelina becomes queen of flower spirits, gets wings, marries king, renamed Maia.

all_stories_flat.title: The Little Mermaid
all_stories_flat.full_story: Far out in the ocean, where the water is as blue as the prettiest cornflower and as clear as crystal, it is very deep. There dwell the Sea King and his subjects. The Sea King's palace is made of coral. His old mother keeps house, proud of noble birth, with six sea-princesses, youngest the Little Mermaid, with beautiful voice. She is 15, may rise to surface. She sees prince on ship, storm sinks ship, she saves prince, falls in love. She visits Sea Witch who lives in creepy forest of polyps, gives her voice in exchange for human legs, each step feels like walking on knives. She drinks potion, tail becomes legs, but mute. Prince finds her, loves her as child but loves another princess he thinks saved him. Little Mermaid has chance to kill prince with knife given by sisters who traded hair to witch, to become mermaid again. She cannot, throws knife, throws herself into sea, becomes foam, but becomes daughter of air, earning soul after 300 years of good deeds. Moral on selfless love.
all_stories_flat.moral: Andersen's tales teach compassion, resilience, and Christian hope
all_stories_flat.source: H.C. Andersen - Public Domain, translation H.P. Paull 1872

all_stories_flat.title: The Emperor's New Clothes
all_stories_flat.full_story: An emperor loves fine clothes. Two swindlers claim to be weavers who can make cloth invisible to stupid or unfit. Emperor pays gold. Swindlers pretend weave on empty looms. Emperor sends old minister who sees nothing but pretends to see to not seem stupid. Emperor himself sees nothing but pretends. He parades naked in supposed clothes. Crowd pretends to admire until child shouts 'But he has nothing on!' Everyone laughs, emperor continues naked parade because cannot admit.
all_stories_flat.moral: Andersen's tales teach compassion, resilience, and Christian hope
all_stories_flat.source: H.C. Andersen - Public Domain, translation H.P. Paull 1872

all_stories_flat.full_story: It is bitter cold New Year's Eve, snowing. Little poor girl sells matches, no one buys, afraid to go home father will beat. She lights bundle to keep grandmother, grandmother takes her to heaven. Next morning, frozen body found with smile, matches burnt. Moral: neglect of poor.

all_stories_flat.title: The Ugly Duckling
all_stories_flat.full_story: A mother duck's eggs hatch, one egg larger, hatches last, ugly gray duckling mocked by all farmyard: ducks, hens, turkey cock. He runs away, meets wild ducks, hunters, old woman with cat and hen, all mock. Winter comes, he freezes in pond, farmer saves. Spring, he sees swans, ashamed to approach, looks in water, sees he is beautiful swan, not ugly duckling. Children cry 'new swan is most beautiful!' He was swan egg hatched in duck nest. Moral: beauty grows with hardship.

all_stories_flat.title: The Snow Queen
all_stories_flat.full_story: Devil made magic mirror that makes beautiful look ugly. Goblins break it, splinters fly into eyes and hearts making people cold. Kay and Gerda are friends. Splinter enters Kay's eye and heart, he becomes cold, mocks Gerda. Snow Queen, beautiful woman of ice and snow, kisses Kay (two kisses make forget Gerda, third would kill), takes him to palace in Lapland. Gerda searches: talks to river, old woman who combs hair with magic, crows, robber girl with knife, Lapland woman and Finland woman. Finmark, finds Kay in Snow Queen palace trying to spell 'Eternity' with ice pieces, but cannot. Gerda weeps, tears melt heart, removes splinter, Kay weeps removing eye splinter. They return home, now grown-ups, but children in heart.
all_stories_flat.moral: Andersen's tales teach compassion, resilience, and Christian hope

all_stories_flat.title: The Ugly Duckling variant
all_stories_flat.full_story: A mother duck's eggs hatch, one egg larger, hatches last, ugly gray duckling mocked by all farmyard: ducks, hens, turkey cock. He runs away, meets wild ducks, hunters, old woman with cat and hen, all mock. Winter comes, he freezes in pond, farmer saves. Spring, he sees swans, ashamed to approach, looks in water, sees he is beautiful swan, not ugly duckling. Children cry 'new swan is most beautiful!' He was swan egg hatched in duck nest. Moral: beauty grows with hardship.

all_stories_flat.title: The Little Mermaid and more
all_stories_flat.full_story: Far out in the ocean, where the water is as blue as the prettiest cornflower and as clear as crystal, it is very deep. There dwell the Sea King and his subjects. The Sea King's palace is made of coral. His old mother keeps house, proud of noble birth, with six sea-princesses, youngest the Little Mermaid, with beautiful voice. She is 15, may rise to surface. She sees prince on ship, storm sinks ship, she saves prince, falls in love. She visits Sea Witch who lives in creepy forest of polyps, gives her voice in exchange for human legs, each step feels like walking on knives. She drinks potion, tail becomes legs, but mute. Prince finds her, loves her as child but loves another princess he thinks saved him. Little Mermaid has chance to kill prince with knife given by sisters who traded hair to witch, to become mermaid again. She cannot, throws knife, throws herself into sea, becomes foam, but becomes daughter of air, earning soul after 300 years of good deeds. Moral on selfless love.
all_stories_flat.moral: Andersen's tales teach compassion, resilience, and Christian hope
all_stories_flat.source: H.C. Andersen - Public Domain, translation H.P. Paull 1872

all_stories_flat.title: The Little Match Seller
all_stories_flat.full_story: It is bitter cold New Year's Eve, snowing. Little poor girl sells matches, no one buys, afraid to go home father will beat. She sits in alley, lights match to warm, sees vision of warm stove. Lights second, sees roast goose. Third, Christmas tree. Fourth, loving grandmother dead. She lights bundle to keep grandmother, grandmother takes her to heaven. Next morning, frozen body found with smile, matches burnt. Moral: neglect of poor.

all_stories_flat.title: The Little Mermaid full
all_stories_flat.full_story: Far out in the ocean, where the water is as blue as the prettiest cornflower and as clear as crystal, it is very deep. There dwell the Sea King and his subjects. The Sea King's palace is made of coral. His old mother keeps house, proud of noble birth, with six sea-princesses, youngest the Little Mermaid, with beautiful voice. She is 15, may rise to surface. She sees prince on ship, storm sinks ship, she saves prince, falls in love. She visits Sea Witch who lives in creepy forest of polyps, gives her voice in exchange for human legs, each step feels like walking on knives. She drinks potion, tail becomes legs, but mute. Prince finds her, loves her as child but loves another princess he thinks saved him. Little Mermaid has chance to kill prince with knife given by sisters who traded hair to witch, to become mermaid again. She cannot, throws knife, throws herself into sea, becomes foam, but becomes daughter of air, earning soul after 300 years of good deeds. Moral on selfless love.
all_stories_flat.moral: Andersen's tales teach compassion, resilience, and Christian hope
all_stories_flat.source: H.C. Andersen - Public Domain, translation H.P. Paull 1872

all_stories_flat.title: The Snow Queen full
all_stories_flat.full_story: Devil made magic mirror that makes beautiful look ugly. Goblins break it, splinters fly into eyes and hearts making people cold. Kay and Gerda are friends. Splinter enters Kay's eye and heart, he becomes cold, mocks Gerda. Snow Queen, beautiful woman of ice and snow, kisses Kay (two kisses make forget Gerda, third would kill), takes him to palace in Lapland. Gerda searches: talks to river, old woman who combs hair with magic, crows, robber girl with knife, Lapland woman and Finland woman. Finmark, finds Kay in Snow Queen palace trying to spell 'Eternity' with ice pieces, but cannot. Gerda weeps, tears melt heart, removes splinter, Kay weeps removing eye splinter. They return home, now grown-ups, but children in heart.

all_stories_flat.title: The Little Mermaid final
all_stories_flat.full_story: Far out in the ocean, where the water is as blue as the prettiest cornflower and as clear as crystal, it is very deep. There dwell the Sea King and his subjects. The Sea King's palace is made of coral. His old mother keeps house, proud of noble birth, with six sea-princesses, youngest the Little Mermaid, with beautiful voice. She is 15, may rise to surface. She sees prince on ship, storm sinks ship, she saves prince, falls in love. She visits Sea Witch who lives in creepy forest of polyps, gives her voice in exchange for human legs, each step feels like walking on knives. She drinks potion, tail becomes legs, but mute. Prince finds her, loves her as child but loves another princess he thinks saved him. Little Mermaid has chance to kill prince with knife given by sisters who traded hair to witch, to become mermaid again. She cannot, throws knife, throws herself into sea, becomes foam, but becomes daughter of air, earning soul after 300 years of good deeds. Moral on selfless love.
all_stories_flat.moral: Andersen's tales teach compassion, resilience, and Christian hope
all_stories_flat.source: H.C. Andersen - Public Domain, translation H.P. Paull 1872

all_stories_flat.title: The Little Match Girl full story
all_stories_flat.full_story: It is bitter cold New Year's Eve, snowing. Little poor girl sells matches, no one buys, afraid to go home father will beat. She sits in alley, lights match to warm, sees vision of warm stove. Lights second, sees roast goose. Third, Christmas tree. Fourth, loving grandmother dead. She lights bundle to keep grandmother, grandmother takes her to heaven. Next morning, frozen body found with smile, matches burnt. Moral: neglect of poor.
all_stories_flat.moral: Andersen's tales teach compassion, resilience, and Christian hope
all_stories_flat.source: H.C. Andersen - Public Domain, translation H.P. Paull 1872

all_stories_flat.title: Apannaka Jataka - The Unreliable & Reliable
all_stories_flat.full_story: Bodhisatta tale: Tortoise friends with two geese. Lake drying, geese say will fly to other lake. Tortoise wants to go. Geese say hold stick in mouth, we carry stick, but don't speak. Tortoise agrees. Children below shout 'See tortoise flying!' Tortoise angry wants to reply 'Shut up!' Opens mouth, falls and dies. Moral: Keep mouth shut, follow advice, don't talk when should be silent.
all_stories_flat.moral: Paramita perfection - Dana, Sila, Kshanti etc.

all_stories_flat.title: Vessantara Jataka - The Prince Who Gave Everything
all_stories_flat.full_story: Vessantara, last birth before Buddha, was prince renowned for generosity. He had magic elephant that brings rain, gave it to enemy kingdom suffering drought. People angry, king Vessantara's father banishes him. Vessantara leaves with wife Maddi and two children Jali and Kanhajina. On way gives away carriage, horses. Lives in Vamka mountain hermitage. Brahmin Jujaka, cruel old man, asks for children as servants. Vessantara gives children, though heart breaks, as ultimate Dana Paramita perfection of generosity. Sakka as Indra tests him asking for wife Maddi, he gives. Sakka returns wife. Jujaka brings children to city, grandfather King Sanjaya ransoms grandchildren, Jujaka dies overeating. Vessantara returns as king. This Jataka taught for centuries, illustrates perfect charity. Moral: Supreme generosity leads to Buddhahood.
all_stories_flat.moral: Paramita perfection - Dana, Sila, Kshanti etc.

all_stories_flat.title: Sibi Jataka - King Sibi and Dove
all_stories_flat.full_story: King Sibi (Sivi) famous for self-sacrifice. Indra as hawk and Agni as dove test him. Dove flies to Sibi's lap seeking refuge from hawk. Hawk says 'Dove is my food, give me.' Sibi says 'I must protect refugee.' Hawk: 'Then give equal weight of your flesh.' Sibi cuts flesh from thigh, puts on scale, dove always heavier. Finally Sibi himself sits on scale giving whole body. Gods reveal themselves, heal him, bless. Moral: King protects even small creature at cost of self.
all_stories_flat.moral: Paramita perfection - Dana, Sila, Kshanti etc.

all_stories_flat.title: Chaddanta Jataka - Six-Tusked Elephant
all_stories_flat.full_story: Bodhisatta born as Chaddanta, chief of 8000 elephants, six-tusked white elephant, with two wives Mahasubhadda and Cullasubhadda. Cullasubhadda jealous of Mahasubhadda. She prays to be queen in next life to kill Chaddanta. Reborn as queen of Benares, feigns illness, says only six-tusked elephant tusks will cure. King sends hunter Sonuttara, who after 7 years finds Chaddanta. Chaddanta, seeing hunter tired, feeds him. Hunter shoots Chaddanta with poison arrow. Chaddanta, though dying, helps hunter cut tusks, not angry, forgives queen. Queen sees tusks, realizes his forgiveness, dies of remorse. Moral: Forgiveness even to murderer - Kshanti Paramita.

all_stories_flat.title: Nigrodha Jataka - Banyan Deer
all_stories_flat.full_story: Bodhisatta born as Banyan Deer King, golden deer with herd of 500, rival herd Sakha with 500. King of Benares hunts daily. Deer kings agree to send one deer daily by lot to king's kitchen to avoid whole herd slaughter. One day lot falls on pregnant doe in Sakha's herd, she begs Sakha, Sakha refuses, she goes to Bodhisatta Banyan deer. Bodhisatta says 'Go, I will go in your place.' Bodhisatta goes to execution block. Cook sees golden deer, reports king. King asks why. Banyan deer speaks: 'I came for doe.' King moved by sacrifice, spares all deer, grants abhaya dana - safety to all animals. Moral: Compassionate king self-sacrifice.

all_stories_flat.title: Vessantara - Last of Ten Great Jatakas
all_stories_flat.full_story: Vessantara, last birth before Buddha, was prince renowned for generosity. He had magic elephant that brings rain, gave it to enemy kingdom suffering drought. People angry, king Vessantara's father banishes him. Vessantara leaves with wife Maddi and two children Jali and Kanhajina. On way gives away carriage, horses. Lives in Vamka mountain hermitage. Brahmin Jujaka, cruel old man, asks for children as servants. Vessantara gives children, though heart breaks, as ultimate Dana Paramita perfection of generosity. Sakka as Indra tests him asking for wife Maddi, he gives. Sakka returns wife. Jujaka brings children to city, grandfather King Sanjaya ransoms grandchildren, Jujaka dies overeating. Vessantara returns as king. This Jataka taught for centuries, illustrates perfect charity. Moral: Supreme generosity leads to Buddhahood.
all_stories_flat.moral: Paramita perfection - Dana, Sila, Kshanti etc.

all_stories_flat.title: Sivi Jataka - King Sivi Gives Eyes
all_stories_flat.full_story: King Sibi (Sivi) famous for self-sacrifice. Indra as hawk and Agni as dove test him. Dove flies to Sibi's lap seeking refuge from hawk. Hawk says 'Dove is my food, give me.' Sibi says 'I must protect refugee.' Hawk: 'Then give equal weight of your flesh.' Sibi cuts flesh from thigh, puts on scale, dove always heavier. Finally Sibi himself sits on scale giving whole body. Gods reveal themselves, heal him, bless. Moral: King protects even small creature at cost of self.
all_stories_flat.moral: Paramita perfection - Dana, Sila, Kshanti etc.

all_stories_flat.title: Sasa Jataka - The Hare and Moon
all_stories_flat.full_story: Once Bodhisatta was born as a hare. He lived with monkey, jackal, otter. They decided to keep Uposatha fast. A Brahmin (Sakka in disguise) came begging food. Monkey gave mangoes, otter fish, jackal stolen meat, but hare had only grass which Brahmin cannot eat. So hare said 'Use me as food' and jumped into fire. Sakka revealed himself, did not let hare burn, took hare and painted his image on moon for all to see. Hence moon has hare. Moral: Perfect self-sacrifice Dana Paramita.
all_stories_flat.moral: Paramita perfection - Dana, Sila, Kshanti etc.

all_stories_flat.title: Sivi Jataka variant
all_stories_flat.full_story: King Sibi (Sivi) famous for self-sacrifice. Indra as hawk and Agni as dove test him. Dove flies to Sibi's lap seeking refuge from hawk. Hawk says 'Dove is my food, give me.' Sibi says 'I must protect refugee.' Hawk: 'Then give equal weight of your flesh.' Sibi cuts flesh from thigh, puts on scale, dove always heavier. Finally Sibi himself sits on scale giving whole body. Gods reveal themselves, heal him, bless. Moral: King protects even small creature at cost of self.
all_stories_flat.moral: Paramita perfection - Dana, Sila, Kshanti etc.

Geese say hold stick in mouth, we carry stick, but don't speak. Tortoise agrees. Children below shout 'See tortoise flying!' Tortoise angry wants to reply 'Shut up!' Opens mouth, falls and dies. Moral: Keep mouth shut, follow advice, don't talk when should be silent.

Geese say hold stick in mouth, we carry stick, but don't speak. Tortoise agrees. Children below shout 'See tortoise flying!' Tortoise angry wants to reply 'Shut up!' Opens mouth, falls and dies. Moral: Keep mouth shut, follow advice, don't talk when should be silent.
all_stories_flat.moral: Paramita perfection - Dana, Sila, Kshanti etc.
all_stories_flat.source: Pali Canon - Khuddaka Nikaya - Jataka - E.B. Cowell translation public domain
all_stories_flat.nirvana_virtue: Dana, Sila, Nekkhamma, Panna, Viriya, Khanti, Sacca, Adhitthana, Metta, Upekkha
